```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
```

Between 2007 and 2009, researchers collected data on over 340 brush-tailed penguins, or penguins of the genus *Pygoscelis*. Dr. Kristen Gorman led the study as part of the Palmer Long Term Ecological Research (Palmer LTER) program, a program funded by the US National Science Foundation (NSF) to research the Antarctic pelagic marine ecosystem. The researchers collected measurements of three species of *Pygoscelis* penguins—Adélie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo penguins—nesting on three islands in the Palmer Archipelago in Antarctica [@gorman2014; @palmerpenguins].

![](lter_penguins.png)

:::::::: cr-section

The penguins were observed on Biscoe Island, Dream Island, and Torgersen Island. @cr-islands

::: {#cr-islands}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 2.5

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(island)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#A6CEE3") +
  labs(x = "Island",
       y = "count") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.line = element_line(color = "black"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(family = "Times New Roman",
                                   size = 12),
        axis.text.y = element_text(family = "Times New Roman",
                                   size = 12),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 15,
                                    margin = margin(t = 8)),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 15,
                                    margin = margin(r = 8)),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#F3F4F6", color = NA),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFFFF", color = NA),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "#E5E7EB",
                                    linewidth = 1),
        plot.margin = margin(t = 15,
                             r = 15,
                             b = 15,
                             l = 15)) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = 0.8)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 20))


```
:::

Gentoo penguins were observed only on Biscoe Island. @cr-islands-gentoo

::: {#cr-islands-gentoo}

                                    margin = margin(r = 8)),

The data include a bit more Adélie than Gentoo penguins, and fewer Chinstrap penguins. Within each species, there is a balance of male and female penguins. @cr-species-sex

::: {#cr-species-sex}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 2.5



penguins |>
  drop_na(species, sex) |>
  count(species, sex, name = "n") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = sex)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n),
             shape = 22,
             fill = "#A6CEE3",
             colour = "#A6CEE3") +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 15) +
  labs(x = "Species",
       y = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.line = element_line(color = "black"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(family = "Times New Roman",
                                   size = 12),
        axis.text.y = element_text(family = "Times New Roman",
                                   size = 12),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 15,
                                    margin = margin(t = 8)),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 15,
                                    margin = margin(r = 8)),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#F3F4F6", color = NA),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFFFF", color = NA),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "#E5E7EB",
                                    linewidth = 1),

                             r = 15,
                             b = 15,
                             l = 15)) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = 0.75)) +
  scale_y_discrete(expand = expansion(add = 0.75))


```

::::::::

### Let's explore how the species physically differ from one another.

::::::::::: cr-section
First, let's look at the penguins' body measurements. @cr-body-flipper

::: {#cr-body-flipper}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 2.5

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point(fill = "#A6CEE3",
             colour = "#A6CEE3",
             size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Flipper Length (mm)",
       y = "Body Mass (g)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.line = element_line(color = "black"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(family = "Times New Roman",
                                   size = 12),
        axis.text.y = element_text(family = "Times New Roman",
                                   size = 12),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 15,
                                    margin = margin(t = 8)),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 15,
                                    margin = margin(r = 8)),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#F3F4F6", color = NA),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFFFF", color = NA),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "#E5E7EB",
                                    linewidth = 1),
        plot.margin = margin(t = 15,
                             r = 15,
                             b = 15,
                             l = 15)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(180, 200, 220),
                     limits = c(165, 240),
                     expand = expansion(add = 0.75)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(3000, 4000, 5000, 6000),
                     limits = c(2250, 6750),
                     expand = expansion(add = 0.75))


```
:::

Gentoo penguins are the largest, with greater body mass and longer flippers than the other two species. @cr-body-flipper-gentoo

::: {#cr-body-flipper-gentoo}

So body size distinguishes Gentoo penguins from the rest, but we can't tell apart Adélie and Chinstrap penguins based on body mass and flipper length alone. @cr-body-flipper

Now let's look at the penguins' bill measurements. @cr-bill

::: {#cr-bill}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 2.5

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(fill = "#A6CEE3",
             colour = "#A6CEE3",
             size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Bill Length (mm)",
       y = "Bill Depth (mm)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        axis.line = element_line(color = "black"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(family = "Times New Roman",
                                   size = 12),
        axis.text.y = element_text(family = "Times New Roman",
                                   size = 12),
        axis.title.x = element_text(size = 15,
                                    margin = margin(t = 8)),
        axis.title.y = element_text(size = 15,
                                    margin = margin(r = 8)),
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#F3F4F6", color = NA),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#FFFFFF", color = NA),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "#E5E7EB",
                                    linewidth = 1),
        plot.margin = margin(t = 15,
                             r = 15,
                             b = 15,
                             l = 15)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(30, 40, 50, 60),
                     limits = c(29, 62.5),
                     expand = expansion(add = 0.75)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(14, 16, 18, 20, 22),
                     limits = c(13, 22),
                     expand = expansion(add = 0.75))


```
:::

Chinstrap penguins tend to have the largest bills, with long and deep bills. @cr-bill-chinstrap

So, bill length and depth separate all three species: Chinstraps have long, deep bills, Adélies have short, deep bills, and Gentoo have long, shallow bills. Body size distinguishes Gentoos, and bill shape can distinguish the rest. @cr-bill
